concepts.name: Range
concepts.description: The range is the simplest measure of spread: the highest value minus the lowest.

concepts.name: Variance
concepts.description: Variance is the average of the squared deviations of each value from the mean.

concepts.name: Standard deviation
concepts.description: Standard deviation is the square root of the variance, bringing the units back to match the original data.

concepts.name: Mean deviation
concepts.description: Mean deviation is the average of the absolute (unsigned) deviations from the mean.

concepts.name: Coefficient of variation
concepts.description: The coefficient of variation expresses spread as a percentage of the mean, making it possible to compare the variability of different data sets.

formulas.title: Range
formulas.prompt: How do you calculate the range of a data set?
formulas.explanation: The range only looks at the two extreme values, ignoring everything in between.
formulas.commonMistake: Including values other than the maximum and minimum in the calculation.

formulas.title: Variance
formulas.prompt: How do you calculate the variance of a data set?
formulas.explanation: Squaring the deviations makes them all positive and gives more weight to values further from the mean.
formulas.commonMistake: Forgetting to square the deviations, or forgetting to divide by n at the end.

formulas.title: Standard deviation
formulas.prompt: How do you find the standard deviation once you know the variance?
formulas.explanation: Taking the square root returns the measure of spread to the same units as the original data.
formulas.commonMistake: Reporting the variance itself instead of taking its square root.
formulas.applicationPrompt: If the variance of a data set is 8, find its standard deviation.

formulas.title: Mean deviation
formulas.prompt: How do you calculate the mean deviation of a data set?
formulas.explanation: Unlike variance, this uses the absolute value of each deviation rather than squaring it.
formulas.commonMistake: Forgetting to take the absolute value, letting negative and positive deviations cancel out.

formulas.title: Coefficient of variation
formulas.prompt: How do you calculate the coefficient of variation, and why is it useful?
formulas.explanation: Because it is a percentage of the mean, the CV lets you compare the relative spread of two data sets even if they use different units or have very different means.
formulas.commonMistake: Comparing raw standard deviations directly when the two data sets have very different means.
formulas.applicationPrompt: A data set has mean 50 and standard deviation 5. Find its coefficient of variation.

formulas.title: Variance without deviations
formulas.prompt: Is there a quicker way to variance than squaring each deviation?
formulas.formula: Variance = (mean of the squares) − (square of the mean)
formulas.explanation: Expanding Σ(x − x̄)² gives Σx² − n x̄², so the deviations are not needed.
formulas.example: 2, 4, 6: mean of squares (4 + 16 + 36)/3 = 56/3, square of the mean 16, variance 8/3.
formulas.commonMistake: Squaring the sum instead of summing the squares.

formulas.title: Shifting and scaling the spread
formulas.prompt: Every value is multiplied by k and then has c added. What is the new standard deviation?
formulas.formula:
New SD = |k| × old SD
Adding c changes nothing
formulas.explanation: Adding moves every value together; multiplying stretches the gaps.
formulas.example: SD of marks 8; each mark × 1.5 + 10: new SD 12.
formulas.commonMistake: Adding c to the standard deviation too.
formulas.applicationPrompt: The SD of temperatures is 5 °C. What is it in °F (F = 1.8C + 32)?

levels.title: How Spread Out Is the Data?
levels.description: The mean tells you the centre; dispersion tells you how far the data spreads around it.

blocks.title: Two data sets, same mean, different spread
blocks.body: Both {5,5,5,5,5} and {1,3,5,7,9} have a mean of 5, but they look very different. The range, variance and standard deviation all describe how spread out the values are around that mean.

blocks.title: Range and variance
blocks.body:
Range = max − min
Variance = average of the squared deviations from the mean
blocks.caption: Range only uses two values; variance uses every value.

blocks.body: Standard deviation is just √variance — it brings the units back to match the original data.

questions.question: What is the range of 5, 12, 7, 20, 3?
questions.method: Subtract the smallest value from the largest.

hints.text: Find the maximum and minimum values first.

commonMistakes: Using values other than the true maximum and minimum.

questions.question: The range of a data set measures

options.text: the average distance of every value from the mean
the spread between the highest and lowest values only
the middle value once the data is sorted

questions.explanation: The range only uses the two extreme values — the maximum and the minimum — and ignores everything in between.
questions.method: Range depends only on the two extreme values.

hints.text: Range does not use every value in the data set.

commonMistakes: Confusing the range with the mean deviation, which does use every value.

questions.question: What is the range of 100, 85, 92, 78, 110?
questions.method: Identify the largest and smallest values.

hints.text: Scan the whole list for the true maximum and minimum.

commonMistakes: Missing the true minimum or maximum by scanning too quickly.

questions.question: A data set has a maximum of 45 and a minimum of 12. What is its range?
questions.method: Subtract the minimum from the maximum.

questions.question: The variance of a data set is calculated as

options.text: the average of the squared deviations from the mean
the square root of the mean
the largest deviation from the mean

questions.explanation: Variance is the average of the squared distances of each value from the mean.
questions.method: Variance squares every deviation before averaging them.

hints.text: Variance involves squaring, not just averaging the raw values.

commonMistakes: Confusing variance with the mean itself.

questions.question: What is the variance of 2, 4, 6, 8, 10?
questions.explanation: Mean = 6. Deviations: −4,−2,0,2,4. Squared: 16,4,0,4,16, summing to 40. Variance = 40 ÷ 5 = 8.
questions.method: Find the mean, then the average of the squared deviations from it.

hints.text: Find the mean first, then work out each deviation.

commonMistakes: Forgetting to square the deviations before averaging.

questions.question: The variance of a data set is 8. What is its standard deviation, to 2 decimal places?
questions.method: Take the square root of the variance.

hints.text: Do not report the variance itself as the standard deviation.

questions.question: What is the mean deviation of 10, 12, 14, 16, 18?
questions.explanation: Mean = 14. Absolute deviations: 4,2,0,2,4, summing to 12. Mean deviation = 12 ÷ 5 = 2.4.
questions.method: Average the unsigned (absolute) deviations from the mean.

hints.text: Use absolute values, not the deviations' original signs.

commonMistakes: Letting the negative and positive deviations cancel out to zero.

questions.question: A data set has mean 50 and standard deviation 5. What is its coefficient of variation, as a percentage?
questions.method: Divide the standard deviation by the mean, then convert to a percentage.

hints.text: CV is always expressed as a percentage.

questions.question: Data set A has mean 80 and SD 8 (CV = 10%). Data set B has mean 60 and SD 9 (CV = 15%). Which data set is more consistent (less variable)?
questions.explanation: A lower coefficient of variation means less relative spread. Since A's CV (10%) is lower than B's (15%), A is more consistent.
questions.method: Compare the coefficients of variation, not the raw standard deviations.

hints.text: Comparing raw SDs (8 vs 9) would be misleading since the means differ.

commonMistakes: Comparing the raw standard deviations (8 vs 9) instead of the CVs.

questions.question: The data set 4, 8, x, 12 has a mean of 8. What is the variance of the completed data set?
questions.explanation: Since the mean is 8, the sum must be 32, so 4+8+x+12 = 24+x = 32, giving x = 8. The data set is 4, 8, 8, 12: deviations −4,0,0,4; squared 16,0,0,16, summing to 32. Variance = 32 ÷ 4 = 8.
questions.method: Find the missing value from the mean first, then compute the variance.

hints.text: You need the complete data set before you can find the variance.

commonMistakes: Trying to compute variance before finding x.

questions.question: A data set has standard deviation 6 and mean 30. What is its coefficient of variation, as a percentage?
questions.method: Divide the SD by the mean, then express as a percentage.

hints.text: This is a direct application of the CV formula.

commonMistakes: Dividing the mean by the SD instead of the other way round.

questions.question: A data set has a variance of 16. If every value in the data set is increased by 5, what is the new variance?
questions.explanation: Adding the same constant to every value shifts the mean by that constant too, so every deviation from the mean stays exactly the same. The variance is unchanged: 16.
solutionSteps: Adding a constant shifts every value and the mean equally.
Deviations from the mean are unchanged.
questions.method: Variance measures spread, which does not change when every value shifts by the same amount.

hints.text: Think about what happens to the deviations from the mean, not the values themselves.

commonMistakes: Assuming the variance also increases by 5, confusing it with the mean.
